nodes.quote: In order to learn about a system, we have to disturb it and change it. This is to ensure cause and effect.
nodes.note: Same line continues: 'To disturb the system, we change several factors. When we make these changes, we say that we have run an experiment.'

nodes.quote: When we perform an experiment, we call it a run.
An important aspect about the outcome is that it is always measurable--in some way.
nodes.note: Line 297 equates outcome and response; RSM line 18 writes it as y.

nodes.quote: A qualitative outcome might also be a description of what happened, for example,
nodes.note: Same line gives the flower colour example (light red, red, dark red).

nodes.quote: which combines an outcome and the need to adjust that outcome.
nodes.note: The book stresses an objective is optional (line 309); the definition does not contradict that, but see the experiment HAS objective edge.

nodes.quote: is the thing you can change to influence the outcome.
nodes.note: The book's synonym is 'variables'; the alias 'input' is not used in the book (harmless).

nodes.quote: Numeric factors are quantified by measuring, such as giving 15 mL of water or 30 mL of water to the plant each day.
Categorical factors usually take on a limited number of values.
nodes.note: Book hedges with 'usually'; line 329 adds that most categorical factors can be converted to numeric ones with careful thought.

nodes.quote: In this section we consider the case when these factors are at two levels.
nodes.note: Low and high levels with the minus and plus signs appear in the table at using-two-levels-for-two-or-more-factors.rst:16; the -1/+1 coding is at analysis-by-least-squares-modelling.rst:30-33.

nodes.quote: you must disturb your system, and then observe it. This is the principle of causality, or
nodes.note: 'Only by intentional manipulation' is line 28; line 63 says designed experiments are the only way to be sure correlated events are causal.

nodes.quote: That is why happenstance data cannot be relied on to imply cause and effect.
nodes.definition: Everyday operating data, collected without intentional changes to the system; it is confounded by other events, so it cannot be relied on to imply cause and effect.
nodes.note: Graph says it 'cannot show' cause and effect; the book is softer: it 'does not always help, because it is confounded by other events' (line 28) and 'cannot be relied on to imply' causality (line 57).

nodes.quote: Feedback control systems keep the region of operation to a small zone.
nodes.note: Same line: 'data collected from such systems has low information quality.'

nodes.quote: some observable association is usually present when there is a causal link, but the association on its own is not sufficient evidence of it.
nodes.definition: Two variables moving together. Some association is usually present when there is a causal link, but on its own it is not sufficient evidence of causality.
nodes.note: Calling correlation 'necessary' for causality contradicts the book: the same line says association is only 'usually' present and that a genuine causal effect can show near-zero linear correlation when the relationship is curved or mechanisms offset.

nodes.quote: learning from and improving a system is an iterative process. It usually follows this cycle:
nodes.note: Steps at lines 14-17. The book says the cycle is 'described' in Box, Hunter and Hunter, not introduced there (see edge). The line calls BHH 'the first reference', but the reference list (examples-of-how-designed-experiments-are-used.rst:34-35) now starts with Fisher: a stale cross-reference in the book.

nodes.quote: Make a conjecture (hypothesis), which we believe is true.
nodes.note: Consequences tested by experiment: lines 15-16. Only taught as one step of the learning cycle.

nodes.quote: One of the most frequent reasons we experiment is to fix a problem with our process.
nodes.note: Same line: 'thereby learn more about our system while fixing the problem.'

nodes.quote: and time-dependent effects (catalyst deactivation, fouling), will impact the response.
nodes.note: The sentence sits in 'Characterization of disturbances' under DOE_blocking_section (line 1), not under DOE-Blocking-and-confounding (line 27). Also why-learning-about-systems-is-important.rst:59 (time-based effects, randomize).

nodes.quote: The general guidance is to choose the low and high values at the edges of normal operation.
nodes.note: Taught in the full-factorial index page, which has no label. The book adds a second half elsewhere: wide enough to show a difference, not so wide as to move to a different operating regime (using-two-levels-for-two-or-more-factors.rst:11, response-surface-methods.rst:67).

nodes.quote: But two-factor interactions are aliased with three-factor interactions
nodes.definition: Shortest word in the defining relation has five letters: no main effect or two-factor interaction is aliased with another, but two-factor interactions are aliased with three-factor interactions.
nodes.note: Graph omits the 2fi-3fi aliasing and that main effects are clear of 2fi (lines 37-40). 'Good for optimizing' is line 35, but line 42 qualifies it: many optimizations succeed with resolution IV.

nodes.quote: Experiments are not a one-shot operation. They are almost always sequential, as we learn more and more about our system.
nodes.note: Also general-approach-for-experimentation.rst:13 ('experiments are never run in one go') and the index entry at line 8.

nodes.quote: We achieved this by building successive least squares models that approximate the underlying surface.
nodes.note: Purpose stated at line 18; sequential at line 24. Book adds 'taking into account any constraints' (line 18).

nodes.quote: As we map out the unknown response surface of

nodes.note: Same line: 'determine where to place your sequential experiments'. Line 494 also uses it when interactions are large.

For example we can achieve a higher production rate, but it is at the expense of more energy.
nodes.note: The RSM sidebar only introduces it; the chapter now has a whole section on it (multi-response-optimization.rst), which is where it is taught.

nodes.quote: One way to balance all competing objectives is to rephrase the
nodes.note: Same line: 'in terms of total costs, or better still, net profit'. The new section adds the condition it needs: relative values known in advance (multi-response-optimization.rst:17-18, table line 430).

nodes.quote: This is tremendously helpful when discussing and evaluating alternate operating points, because plant managers and operators can then visually see the trade-offs.
nodes.note: Matches the RSM sidebar. The multi-response section develops this route into the 'sweet spot' (DOE-sweet-spot), which the graph lacks: see missing.

nodes.quote: are handled by fixing them at one or the other value, and then performing the optimization conditional on those selected values.
nodes.note: Also line 500 (alternate a binary factor's sign at a new baseline). Line 458 adds: with categorical factors prefer an optimal design over a Box-Behnken design.

nodes.quote: EVOP is an iterative hunt for the process optimum by making small perturbations to the system.
nodes.note: 'Factorial' is slightly narrow: the same line allows designs that estimate curvature, like the central composite design. Line 548: small ranges because every run must give saleable product.

nodes.quote: Since the process is not constant, the optimum will gradually move away from its current operating point.
nodes.note: Raw-material change comes from general-approach-for-experimentation.rst:43.

nodes.quote: Once you reach the optimum, then second order effects and curvature must be added to assess the direction of the optimum.
nodes.note: The four phases in the current book are: 1 screening (line 20), 2 sequential experiments: foldover, projectivity, higher-resolution fractions (line 30), 3 optimizing (line 36), 4 maintain the optimum with EVOP (line 41). They match the graph. Only the two guidelines at lines 15-16 are attributed to BHH, not the phases. Line 38: phase 3 uses full or half-fraction factorials for steepest ascent.

nodes.quote: You should be always hunting for the process optimum.
do not spend more than 20% to 25% of your time and budget on your first group of experiments.
The best time to run an experiment is after the experiment.
However, it is the high impurity that actually causes the lower yield, not the pressure itself.
nodes.note: Adapted from BHH (line 45, 47).

nodes.quote: How can we determine other settings (factors) that give long shelf life but reduce the energy consumed?
Chapters 5 and 6 with topics from Chapters 11, 12, 13 and 15 are the most heavily used in this chapter.
nodes.note: Listed as 'Strongly recommended', second after Fisher.

nodes.quote: Some examples of the success of EVOP and a review paper are in these readings:
nodes.definition: George Box, Evolutionary Operation: A Method for Increasing Industrial Productivity, Applied Statistics, 1957; a reading the chapter gives on evolutionary operation.
nodes.note: 'Introduced EVOP' is true historically but the book never says it; it lists the paper as a reading (line 552, and the reference list line 38).

edges.quote: Experiment and collect data. Are the consequences that we expected visible in the data?
Make a conjecture (hypothesis), which we believe is true.
Designed experiments are the only way we can be sure that these correlated events are causal.
edges.note: Sharper verb: ESTABLISHES (the book says 'ensure cause and effect', design-analysis-experiments.rst:274).

edges.quote: does not always help, because it is confounded by other events that occur at the same time.
That is why happenstance data cannot be relied on to imply cause and effect.
edges.note: Book's wording is 'cannot be relied on to imply'; CANNOT_ESTABLISH would match it better.

edges.quote: Everyday, happenstance data is limited by feedback control systems.
edges.note: Happenstance data are everyday operating data; feedback control does not create them, it confines operation to a small zone so the data carry little information (line 36).

edges.quote: Pressure is correlated with the yield, but there is no cause-and-effect relationship between them.
edges.note: Sharper: IS_NOT_SUFFICIENT_FOR (line 63).

edges.quote: One of the most frequent reasons we experiment is to fix a problem with our process.
edges.note: The book presents troubleshooting as a reason to experiment; IS_A_PURPOSE_OF would be closer than IS_A.

edges.quote: Every experiment always has an outcome.
All experiments must have at least one factor that is changed.
Every experiment does not have to have an objective, but usually we have an objective in our mind.
edges.note: Beside 'HAS response' and 'HAS factor', which the book makes mandatory, this triple reads as mandatory too; the book says the opposite in so many words.

edges.quote: which combines an outcome and the need to adjust that outcome.
edges.note: USES is vague; SETS_GOAL_FOR states the book's meaning.

edges.quote: Qualitative measurements are also possible.
We distinguish between two types of factors:
We distinguish between two types of factors:
In this section we consider the case when these factors are at two levels.
Categorical variables have no implicit ordering.
edges.note: Line 329: most categorical factors can be converted to numeric ones; a CONVERTIBLE_TO edge would capture that.

edges.quote: we can say "there are eight runs" in the set of experiments.
edges.note: The book uses 'experiment' both for one run (same line) and for the whole set (e.g. 'a 15-run experiment', response-surface-methods.rst:338); the edge uses the second sense, while the experiment node's definition is closer to the first.

edges.quote: Operators, ambient conditions, physical equipment, lab analyses, and time-dependent effects (catalyst deactivation, fouling), will impact the response.
edges.note: The list follows 'External disturbances will always have an effect on our response variable' on the same line.

edges.quote: The general guidance is to choose the low and high values at the edges of normal operation.
Resolution V designs: are good for optimizing
For optimizing a process, learning about complex effects, and developing high-accuracy predictive models
edges.note: Follows from the resolution section, but with two caveats: line 42 says many optimizations succeed with resolution IV, and the phase 3 text itself (general-approach-for-experimentation.rst:38-39) names full or half-fraction factorials for steepest ascent and then curvature terms, which no two-level design estimates.

edges.quote: RSM then is a tool the describes how we should run these sequential sets of experiments.
edges.note: Same line contrasts it with COST: sequential, but changing multiple factors simultaneously.

edges.quote: As we map out the unknown response surface of
edges.note: The book does say 'map out', but RSM never maps the whole surface: it fits successive local models along a path (line 285, 'approximate the underlying surface'). Sharper verb: APPROXIMATES_LOCALLY.

edges.quote: we move our process as close as possible towards the optimum, taking into account any constraints.
edges.note: SEEKS is vague and loses 'subject to constraints'. Sharper verb: MOVES_PROCESS_TOWARDS (line 18) or CONVERGES_ON (line 285).

edges.quote: Perform factorial experiments (full or fractional factorials), completely randomized.
edges.note: Also fractional factorials and, near the optimum, central composite designs (line 506); USES ccd and USES fractional_factorial are missing.

edges.quote: Use the model to estimate the path of steepest ascent (or descent if minimizing
An optimum exhibits curvature, so a model that only has linear terms in it will not be suitable
edges.note: Book's verb is EXHIBITS.

edges.quote: Draw contour plots of this estimated response surface
edges.note: The plot shows the fitted model's surface, an estimate of the unknown one (line 130 contrasts model contours with the true contours 'unknown in practice'). SHOWS_ESTIMATE_OF is more precise.

edges.quote: We get those two values by eye-balling the solid contour lines, drawn from the above non-linear model.
edges.note: Approximately, and only the model's optimum: line 283 says it is close to, not at, the true optimum; line 512 adds it can be found analytically.

edges.quote: One way to balance all competing objectives is to rephrase the
edges.note: REMEDIED_BY treats several responses as a defect; HANDLED_BY is accurate. The new section treats this as one of three approaches and says it needs costs known well enough to combine credibly (multi-response-optimization.rst:17-18); the third approach, desirability, is missing from the graph.

edges.quote: Another way is to superimpose the response surfaces of two or more
edges.note: Use HANDLED_BY. The multi-response section turns this route into the sweet spot: specification boundaries on shared axes (multi-response-optimization.rst:185-188).

edges.quote: Drawing it is a matter of putting both boundaries on the same axes and shading the
edges.note: The boundaries are each response's contour at its specification limit (line 219).

edges.quote: Categorical variables (yes/no, catalyst A or B) are handled by fixing them at one or the other value
Response surface methods generally work best when the variables we adjust are numerically continuous.
Similar to response surface methods, once every iteration is completed, the process is moved towards the optimum.
Evolutionary operation (EVOP) is a tool to help maintain a full-scale process at its optimum.
edges.note: TRACKS is acceptable because the optimum moves; the book's own verbs are MAINTAINS_PROCESS_AT (line 544) and HUNTS_FOR (line 546).

edges.quote: An EVOP program should always be in place on a process, because raw materials change, fouling and catalyst deactivation take place
edges.note: EVOP does not remove the drift; it follows the moving optimum. Sharper: MOTIVATES (process_drift MOTIVATES evop) or COMPENSATED_BY.

edges.quote: Replicate runs are also made to separate the signal from noise, because the optimum region is usually flat.
Chemical processes drift due to things such as heat-exchanger fouling, build-up inside reactors and tubing, catalyst deactivation, and other slowly varying disturbances in the system.
edges.note: The book says drift is due to these slow disturbances, so CAUSED_BY is more exact than IS_A; the two nodes overlap (see overlaps).

edges.quote: using the concepts of evolutionary operation (EVOP).
edges.note: Line 41 is the fourth phase; line 36 is the third.

edges.quote: by exploring the response surface using the important variables discovered in the prior phases.
using the concepts of evolutionary operation (EVOP).
Keep some time aside to add more experiments and learn more about the system.
edges.note: Book derives it from after_the_experiment ('For the above reason'); a budget_rule FOLLOWS_FROM after_the_experiment edge is missing.

edges.quote: The main point is that experiments are never run in one go. You will always have more questions after the first round.
edges.note: Line 13 attributes both guidelines to Box, Hunter and Hunter; no such edge exists.

edges.quote: A line could be drawn through the points from the happenstance measurements, taken from the process at different times in the past.
Pressure is correlated with the yield, but there is no cause-and-effect relationship between them.
For example we can achieve a higher production rate, but it is at the expense of more energy.
edges.note: The book never maps the usage questions to sections, but shelf life against energy is the same trade-off the sidebar describes. A concept does not answer a question: IS_INSTANCE_OF multiple_responses is sharper, and the answering methods are overlay_surfaces, single_combined_response and desirability.

edges.quote: Some examples of the success of EVOP and a review paper are in these readings:
edges.note: Historically true (Box 1957 is the founding EVOP paper), but the book only lists it as a reading. DESCRIBED_IN is what the book supports.

edges.quote: learning from and improving a system is an iterative process. It usually follows this cycle:
edges.note: The line opens 'As described in the first reference, the book by Box, Hunter and Hunter'. BHH describes the cycle; it did not introduce it (the conjecture, consequence, test cycle is the scientific method, and Box wrote about it before BHH). Also the book's 'first reference' is stale: the list now starts with Fisher.

overlaps.note: Both definitions are built on fouling and catalyst deactivation. process_drift is the EVOP-specific consequence (the optimum moves); link them with CAUSED_BY rather than IS_A, or merge.
Phase 4 is defined as 'use EVOP'; the phase node adds nothing beyond its USES edge and the PRECEDES ordering.
Phase 3 restates RSM (explore the response surface, steepest ascent, then curvature terms).
Both describe iterating experiments; the book gives the cycle as the reason experiments are sequential. Link (sequential_experimentation FOLLOWS_FROM learning_cycle) rather than merge.
Distinct guidelines, but the book derives the 20 to 25% rule from the first ('For the above reason', general-approach-for-experimentation.rst:16); add FOLLOWS_FROM.

missing.definition: Grades each response from 0 to 1 and combines the grades by a weighted geometric mean, so one failed specification makes the overall desirability zero.

missing.name: Lack-of-fit test
missing.definition: Splits the residual sum of squares into pure error and lack of fit; a large F-ratio of their mean squares is evidence the model is missing a term.
missing.quote: The idea is to split the model's residual sum of squares into two parts.
